## Editorial policy
# Agentic GRC: Editorial Policy (version 2)

Owner: Iva Biscanic. This policy is supplied to the AI at every editorial stage
(selection, briefs, articles, video scripts). The AI applies it; I review its decisions.

## 1. Audience and purpose
Readers are executives and risk, compliance and security leaders (CEO, COO, CFO, CISO),
consultants and researchers working with critical-infrastructure operators in Europe and the
US. They understand AI and their sector's regulation. They lack a clear view of where current
frameworks fall short for **agentic AI**: systems that plan and act with some autonomy.
Central question: *As AI agents start acting autonomously in critical infrastructure, which
risks are real, which claims are hype, and what do current governance frameworks require
operators to do?*

## 2. Relevance (what we cover)
Accept material that bears directly on at least one of:
- **R1 AI agents in critical-infrastructure operations**: energy, grids, telecom, water,
  transport, OT/ICS; deployment, oversight, failures, controls, vendor access.
- **R2 Rules and frameworks**: EU AI Act, NIS2, Cyber Resilience Act, NIST AI RMF, NIST CSF,
  FERC/NERC CIP, sector regulators, standards (e.g. ISO/IEC 42001), procurement rules.
- **R3 AI data centres as critical infrastructure**: grid connection, reliability standards,
  energy demand, security, local opposition, and what this means for operators.
- **R4 Governance precedents** (not about AI itself): how a regulator turns an emerging-technology
  risk into concrete requirements for critical-infrastructure operators (exposure assessment,
  migration plans, deadlines, verifiable readiness criteria), e.g. quantum-safe migration mandates.
  **Guardrail:** R4 evidence may support only an analogy or inference about AI, labelled as such;
  it must never be the only evidence for a claim about AI systems.
An item counts as R1-R3 only if its text explicitly discusses AI, machine learning or autonomous
agents. General OT or critical-infrastructure security content without AI is R4 or rejected.
AI-enabled attacks on infrastructure are relevant **only** when the item changes what
operators must do to govern their own AI systems; otherwise reject.
Reject: general geopolitics, defence and military dependencies, macro-economic or industrial-policy
debates, consumer AI, product promotions, and AI news with no link to critical infrastructure or
governance. If an item fits none of R1-R4, reject it; do not stretch a category to fit.

## 3. Freshness and novelty
- Only material published within the 30-day window is used (enforced mechanically before
  selection). Publication date and collection date are kept separate.
- **Republished material** (e.g. "Archive" episodes, reposted recordings, refreshed dates on
  old articles) is **deferred** unless it contains something newly reported; the reason must
  say what is old and what, if anything, is new. Titles containing "Archive", "Rewind", "Encore"
  or "Rebroadcast", or an introduction saying the recording is from an earlier date, signal
  republication even when the feed date is new.
- When a recent source discusses an older event, say so and state what is newly learned.
- Several outlets repeating the same announcement count as **one underlying claim**, not
  independent corroboration.

## 4. Credibility (judged per claim, not per source)
- Reputation, popularity or the model's own confidence are never enough on their own.
- Prefer primary evidence: regulator documents, audit findings, incident data, named
  practitioners describing their own experience, published methods.
- **Vendor and commercial content** (e.g. Dragos, IBM, AWS, consultancies) is usable but is a
  `source_claim`: note the commercial incentive and look for independent corroboration.
  A vendor presenting or demonstrating its own platform, product series or service is
  **promotional and rejected**, even when the tone is educational, unless it reports specific,
  checkable results about AI in operations (what was deployed, where, with what outcome or failure).
- Think-tank and podcast opinion is interpretation; label it as such.
- Unsupported claims (no data, no method, no named source) are not used as facts.

## 5. Uncertainty and conflicting evidence
- Distinguish `reported_fact`, `source_claim` and `inference` (my interpretation).
- When sources conflict, present both, explain why they may differ (scope, incentives, data),
  and say what would settle it. Do not invent disagreement where the evidence agrees.
- State remaining uncertainty explicitly. If the evidence does not justify a conclusion,
  say so rather than forcing one.

## 6. Diversity of perspectives
Each piece should draw on at least three independent publishers and, across the series,
on policy/research, industry/vendor and practitioner perspectives, using written, video and
podcast evidence. Known gaps to state openly: operators' own voices, EU regulators and
agencies (e.g. ENISA), workers and affected communities, non-US/EU perspectives.

## 7. Geography
EU and US weighted equally. Prefer evidence that allows a transatlantic comparison.

## 8. Voice
Plain, precise, non-alarmist English for senior professionals. Short paragraphs, no hype
words, no marketing tone. Every substantive claim is traceable to evidence.

## 9. Exclusions
No undated material as evidence. No invented sources, quotes or numbers. No personal data
about private individuals. AI-generated presentation is disclosed.

## Change log
- **v2 (2026-10-18)**, after reviewing live run 1 (docs/review_run1.md). The model accepted a vendor
  platform walkthrough with no AI content that v1 already excluded (after rejecting it in an earlier call),
  and stretched R3 to fit a non-AI regulatory item. Changes: stricter vendor rule (own-platform
  walkthroughs are promotional); R1-R3 require explicit AI content; new R4 for governance precedents
  with a guardrail; "do not stretch a category" rule; concrete republication signals; military
  dependencies and industrial-policy debates added to the reject list.
- **v1 (2026-10-18)**: initial policy.


## The three planned pieces
- 01: What changed, and which developments matter most to this audience?
- 02: Which claims withstand scrutiny, and where are the evidence or interpretations in tension?
- 03: What do these developments imply for the audience, and what should they watch next?

## Task
For EVERY item below, decide:
- "accept": relevant under policy section 2, credible enough to use, and useful for at least
  one piece. Give the piece_ids it would serve.
- "reject": off-topic, promotional without substance, or unusable. piece_ids must be [].
- "defer": possibly relevant but republished/old, duplicative of another item, or too thin to
  use now. piece_ids must be [].
The reason must cite the policy section(s) applied (e.g. "R1; 4 vendor claim") and be specific
to this item: what it contributes, or why it fails. Do not judge credibility by reputation alone.
Also give "credibility_note" (what kind of evidence it offers and any commercial incentive) and
"relevance" (R1, R2, R3 or none).

Singapore prioritizes critical infrastructure in quantum-safe push, funds cryptographic discovery, legacy OT migration The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA) issued quantum-safe migration guidance recommending that organizations exposed to quantum-related cybersecurity risks establish migration plans by 2027 and aim to complete the transition by 2035. The guidance calls for Critical Information Infrastructure (CII) systems to complete migration by 2031, reflecting Singapore’s risk-based approach to preparing for advances in quantum computing that could eventually undermine widely used cryptographic methods protecting digital communications, transactions and sensitive information. The agency also advised organizations to assess their risk exposure, identify critical systems and engage technology vendors and partners to understand available quantum-safe solutions. To support implementation, CSA has launched the Quantum-Safe Kickstarter Grant, which will provide time-limited seed funding for organizations to pilot quantum-safe solutions and address practical migration challenges. Open to all organizations, with priority given to CII owners, the grant will run from Nov. 1, 2026, to Oct. 31, 2027, with each funded pilot lasting up to six months. Priority use cases include end-to-end migration of applications or systems, cryptographic discovery and inventory, and migration of operational technology (OT), legacy and infrastructure-heavy systems. Pilot participants must report their findings and demonstrated impact. Advances in quantum computing could eventually undermine widely used cryptographic methods that protect digital communications, transactions and sensitive information today. Although it remains uncertain when quantum computers will become capable of breaking these methods, organizations need to begin preparing for the transition. CSA recognized that quantum-safe migration is a complex undertaking. Cryptography is embedded across applications, networks, infrastructure and interconnected systems, often involving multiple technology vendors. Organizations will need time to identify their cryptographic dependencies, assess risks, test suitable solutions and implement changes without disrupting their operations. This is particularly important for critical infrastructure and legacy systems, where technology changes must be carefully managed. Singapore has started preparing early for quantum-safe migration, adopting a risk-based approach that prioritises CII systems. In June 2026, CSA issued quantum-safe migration guidance to CII owners with key milestones, including the completion of quantum-safe migration of CII systems by 2031. By preparing early, organizations can manage the transition in a planned and orderly manner, rather than waiting until quantum threats become imminent. As part of Singapore’s efforts to strengthen quantum-safe readiness, CSA has taken two further steps to help organizations move from planning to action. The agency published a new advisory recommending that organizations exposed to quantum-related cybersecurity risks put in place a quantum-safe migration plan by 2027, and aim to complete migration by 2035, the latter being in line with international guidance. These include organizations that hold sensitive information requiring long-term confidentiality, as well as those providing important services such as communications and digital transactions, where maintaining the integrity and confidentiality of information is essential. Additionally, the advisory sets out practical and low-risk steps organizations can take now, including assessing their risk exposure, identifying their most important systems, and engaging technology vendors and partners to understand available quantum-safe solutions. Claroty Team82 shows AI can rebuild Danfoss controller exploits in 28 minutes, putting Internet-facing OT at risk Claroty’s Team82 research team reproduced three previously disclosed vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM 800A refrigeration controllers using an artificial intelligence (AI) coding agent, chaining two of them to achieve root-level command execution on a laboratory device in approximately 28 minutes at an AI usage cost of about US$6. The report detailed that the experiment used Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 4.6 in medium reasoning mode through the Cursor AI-native code editor, with publicly available firmware, vulnerability identifiers and analysis tools. The team found that the agent initially reproduced two vulnerabilities, CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452, but required researcher guidance and Ghidra reverse-engineering integration to correctly reproduce the authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2025-41450 and demonstrate root access. “The agent initially reproduced two vulnerabilities (CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452) but failed to correctly analyze the authentication bypass (CVE-2025-41450), confidently pursuing an incorrect approach,” Amir Zaltzman, vulnerability researcher, wrote in a Team82 blog post last week. “We redirected the investigation and provided a Ghidra Model Context Protocol (MPC) integration for targeted decompilation and cross-reference analysis of the controller’s 67 MB main application binary. Ghidra is a reverse-engineering platform.” He noted that with the right tools and guidance, the agent reproduced the bypass and chained it with command injection to demonstrate root access. “The researcher remained essential, but hands-on analysis was substantially reduced. Human expertise was needed to recognize incorrect results, ask the right questions, and validate the outcome. Once equipped with the appropriate tools and direction, the agent automated much of the subsequent analysis and vulnerability reproduction.” Team82 said the findings highlight how AI coding tools could lower the time, cost and expertise required to reproduce known vulnerabilities affecting operational technology (OT) systems. Searches using Censys and Shodan identified thousands of potentially exposed devices, underscoring the risks associated with internet-facing industrial equipment that attackers may reach without first compromising an organization’s internal network. The research team cautioned that the experiment did not demonstrate autonomous vulnerability discovery from scratch, as it relied on public vulnerability disclosures and human intervention to correct the AI agent’s initial errors. However, the combination of publicly accessible firmware, disclosed vulnerabilities, and limited-cost AI-assisted analysis could shorten the interval between vulnerability disclosure and practical exploit reproduction, increasing security concerns for organizations operating refrigeration controllers and other industrial systems. Using Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 4.6 in medium reasoning mode through the Cursor AI-native code editor, we reproduced the vulnerabilities and chained two of them to achieve root-level command execution on a lab device. The work took about 28 minutes from initial analysis to a working exploit, at a cost of roughly $6 in AI usage. The firmware was downloaded directly from Danfoss’s public website, with no registration or encryption barrier to overcome. The starting point was public CVE identifiers, vulnerability classifications, the firmware package and analysis tools, with no original research or private analysis. published_at: 2026-10-16T10:11:31Z
url: https://industrialcyber.co/utilities-energy-power-water-waste/ampyx-cyber-examines-ferc-2026-cip-audit-findings-on-generator-registration-shared-control-and-ai-access-risks/
excerpt:
Ampyx Cyber examines FERC 2026 CIP audit findings on generator registration, shared control and AI access risks Ampyx Cyber highlighted gaps in generator registration, cyber risk categorization and artificial intelligence (AI) access controls in the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (FERC) 2026 Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) audit findings. Auditors found inverter-based generation resources operating above applicable Bulk Electric System thresholds before registration or required cybersecurity evaluations, as well as cases in which affiliates and third-party service providers monitored or controlled multiple generation resources from shared control centers that met medium-impact criteria, although individual operators had classified their systems as low impact. The FERC report covers non-public CIP audits of several U.S.-based North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) registered entities during fiscal year 2026, which for the federal government ran from October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2026. Staff from NERC and the Regional Entities took part in the virtual and on-site portions. “The top-line finding reads a lot like other years. Most of what the audited entities had in place met the mandatory requirements, potential noncompliance and security risks remained, and staff folded practices the standards don’t require into the report as voluntary recommendations,” Patrick Miller, president and CEO of Ampyx Cyber, wrote in a Thursday company blog post. “The report is short, about twelve pages of substance, and it drops the appendix of prior years’ lessons that the 2025 report carried, pointing to a summary on FERC’s staff reports page instead. I’d read the footnotes closely, because some of the more useful details are down there, including FERC’s count of low and medium impact requirements and the Order No. 693 language on delegation.” Ampyx Cyber also highlighted FERC’s findings on AI tools operating within CIP-networked environments, where auditors generally found appropriate controls but identified differences in how entities managed access. The report notes that AI capabilities are increasingly being incorporated into products and services, potentially complicating compliance as tools gain the ability to monitor networks, respond to threats and perform tasks similar to those of human users. FERC recommends that entities assess the business need for AI tools, manage their access to bulk electric system cyber systems and sensitive information, monitor external communications, and account for AI-related risks in vendor supply chain security programs. The first lesson, on timely registration and CIP compliance for generation resources, falls under CIP-002-5.1a R1. Auditors found that new inverter-based resources (IBRs) entered commercial operation above the Bulk Electric System (BES) threshold before NERC registration or CIP-002 evaluation, which traced to a misreading of the Commercial Operation Date (COD). Miller observed that the threshold is the BES one. published_at: 2026-10-16T10:02:23Z
url: https://industrialcyber.co/news/sans-institute-launches-it-and-ot-training-tracks-to-strengthen-singapores-critical-infrastructure-cybersecurity/
excerpt:
SANS Institute launches IT and OT training tracks to strengthen Singapore’s critical infrastructure cybersecurity SANS Institute launched dedicated training tracks, designed for practitioners across enterprises, including CII sectors to strengthen the capabilities of cybersecurity capabilities in managing advanced persistent threats across critical digital and operational environments. Two specialised pathways have been introduced, including IT Track: Practitioner Technical Programme (SANS): Advanced Persistent Threat Detection and Response for IT Environment; and OT Track: Practitioner Technical Programme (SANS): Advanced Persistent Threat Detection and Response for OT Environment, to equip practitioners with the expertise needed to defend against evolving cyber threats and enhance organisational resilience. The two tracks are built on SANS Institute’s established courses, FOR508: Advanced Incident Response, Threat Hunting, and Digital Forensics and ICS515: ICS Visibility, Detection, and Response. Beyond skill-building for individual cyber practitioners across enterprises, the tracks are designed to lift the baseline readiness of Singapore’s CII sector as a whole, since they help close the visibility gap between enterprise IT and operational systems as CII environments converge, as well as build collective resilience against the evolving threat actors known to target Singapore’s CII. The programmes come as CIIOs in Singapore face sophisticated attacks, including from state-sponsored threat actors. For CIIOs, the programmes support efforts to develop the cybersecurity competencies of personnel responsible for operating and managing CII systems to perform their roles effectively. The programmes also complement the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore’s (CSA) broader efforts to strengthen CII owners’ cybersecurity capabilities and resilience through targeted training and competency development. “As cyber threats become increasingly sophisticated, cybersecurity practitioners need to continually strengthen their capabilities to detect and respond to cyber threats, such as advanced persistent threats. The Practitioner Technical Programme complements these efforts by providing hands-on training opportunities for practitioners to deepen their technical expertise and apply their skills in realistic scenarios,” said Ong Kok Wee, Assistant Chief Executive, Policy and Corporate Development, CSA. “We’re proud to work with CSA to support cybersecurity practitioners across enterprises, including Critical Information Infrastructure Owners in strengthening their cybersecurity capabilities,” said Matthias Chia, regional director for Southeast and North Asia at SANS Institute. “By pairing proven SANS curricula with content shaped to CSA’s specifications, these programmes help organisations ensure the people running critical systems have the skills to keep them secure and resilient.”

excerpt:
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission on Thursday issued proposals aimed at making it easier to develop gas infrastructure, including liquefied natural gas export projects and gas pipelines. In part, the proposals are geared to ensuring that the United States can supply gas-fired power plants with the fuel they need to run, according to FERC Chairman Laura Swett. “Building generation involves gas,” Swett said Thursday during the agency’s monthly meeting. “The only current restriction on getting American gas is our ability to get the gas to market and the infrastructure bottlenecks.” In a move Swett said would address the issue without reducing environmental oversight, FERC on a 4-1 vote proposed no longer requiring air dispersion modeling for its reviews of gas projects under the National Environmental Policy Act. “The Commission will shift to a more streamlined approach, ultimately designed to bring our NEPA analysis ‘back in line with the statutory text and common sense,’ and likewise avoid functional duplication of [Clean Air Act] review and permitting responsibilities entrusted to the [Environmental Protection Agency] and the state air permitting agencies,” FERC said in its draft policy statement. Air dispersion models simulate how a proposed project’s emissions will spread in the atmosphere and interact with background pollution and emissions from nearby sources, FERC said. “The models have proven time and again to be an unnecessary source of confusion, delay and litigation risk,” Swett said. “Air dispersion modeling has proven a tremendous boon for the infrastructure opponents and lawyers who litigate the commission's natural gas authorizations.” FERC Commissioner Judy Chang dissented from the draft policy statement, saying it would make it harder to assess how people may be affected by nearby gas projects. Air dispersion models are “the best tool we have for understanding the likely local and regional air impacts of the projects we permit, outside of actually having physical monitors,” Chang said at the meeting. FERC also proposed a three-tiered blanket authorization framework for LNG projects that would allow certain activities to proceed automatically, without the developer filing an application at the agency. Some activities would require a 60-day notice and comment period and others — such as adding liquefaction trains, LNG tanks and marine berths to an existing plant — would require a 90-day period. The proposal is “rooted in the simple principle that [FERC] should devote our resources to projects that warrant searching scrutiny and provide a more efficient pathway for those that don't,” FERC Commissioner Lindsay See said at the meeting. See spearheaded the idea of creating a blanket authorization program for LNG projects like the one it has for gas pipeline projects. Dive Brief: - Changes to the federal policy landscape and rapid load growth projections have led utilities and developers to recalibrate toward deploying traditional dispatchable resources like natural gas, resulting in clean power growth slowing from its 2024 peak, while fossil capacity — if dispatched as projected — “could reach a market share not seen since the early 2010s,” the Environmental Defense Fund said in a report released Tuesday. - However, the deployment of gas-fired generation faces headwinds, including turbine shortages and the potential for natural gas price volatility, which could drive up the Levelized Cost of Energy for gas plants, the report noted. - “Rising gas turbine costs and supply shortages are already making new gas plants more expensive and slower to build, prompting some developers to consider clean power alternatives that can often come online faster and at a lower cost,” David Villagrana, EDF’s lead counsel for clean energy tax solutions, said in an email to Utility Dive. Dive Insight: While clean energy “continues to account for the largest share of planned U.S. power sector development,” EDF said planned development has slowed while fossil fuel deployments have caught up. “Based on capacity factors, planned natural gas project capacity is now comparable to that for solar and wind,” the report said. An Oct. 8 Wood Mackenzie analysis found that investment in gas generation capacity is entering “a supply deficit cycle through the late 2030s, driven by data centre load growth, a dynamic that keeps thermal capital costs elevated and reinforces the long-term economic case for renewables and storage.” Federal policy changes like coal industry subsidies, repealed greenhouse gas regulations, the rollback of clean energy tax credits and barriers for permitting new clean energy are increasingly incentivizing utilities and developers to pursue fossil fuel generation, the report said. For that reason, Villagrana said, it’s “difficult to predict how much the market will shift,” even as developers encounter barriers to deploying new gas. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which was introduced in the Senate Sept. 30, would prevent the revocation or suspension of previously issued federal permits for energy projects, and create a right for projects to sue over a pattern of “disparate” federal treatment based on project type. Villagrana said EDF “is still reviewing the bill and working with modelers, partners and colleagues to understand its impact.” BAAJA would also speed the federal permitting process by altering the National Environmental Policy Act. Groups like the Sierra Club have criticized aspects of BAAJA, saying it “weakens environmental laws,” while the legislation received strong support from other groups like the Citizens’ Climate Lobby. Fossil generation’s exposure to global risk Fossil fuel project cancellations have also declined at the same time that clean energy cancellations have increased, said EDF’s report. Fossil fuel project cancellations dropped in 2024 and have remained low through the first half of 2026, the report said. title: Battery-powered trains coming to Chicago: a first look
published_at: 2026-10-14T14:17:00Z
url: https://www.utilitydive.com/news/stadler-metra-chicago-battery-electric-train/832993/
excerpt:
Dive Brief: - The Chicago commuter rail system, Metra, and rail vehicle manufacturer Stadler debuted a battery-electric train at the American Public Transportation Association conference and expo in Chicago last week. - Metra has ordered eight of the train sets, which are expected to enter passenger service by 2028, according to a news release. Each train set will consist of four cars with a seating capacity of about 200, a Stadler spokesperson told Smart Cities Dive. - Metra will be able to deploy the battery-powered trains without adding infrastructure along the right-of-way. Metra plans to introduce the train sets along a route between two stations on the Beverly Branch of the Rock Island Line, a distance of 16.4 miles. Dive Insight: Commuter rail operators are exploring battery-electric trains and locomotives. Caltrain, a commuter rail line that serves the San Francisco Peninsula, electrified 51 miles of its route with overhead catenary wire and will add battery-electric trains to run beyond the wired portion of the route. The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority is planning to replace diesel-powered trains with battery power on the Fairmount Commuter Rail Line, which serves an environmental justice community. The New York Metropolitan Transportation Authority ordered 13 battery-electric passenger locomotives to serve trains on its Metro-North lines, marking the first use of the technology in North America. A portion of the Metra train set was on display at the expo. The trains, which will be manufactured in Salt Lake City, are capable of speeds up to 90 mph but will be restricted to 79 mph in use, the spokesperson said. The batteries have a range of about 50 miles, he said, which allows the train to make three runs between the LaSalle Street and Blue Island stations. The trains can be recharged at the terminal stations, the spokesperson said. “These new trainsets are coming at a perfect time,” Northern Illinois Transit Authority Chairman Tom Kotarac said in a statement. “We are excited about the potential for these new trainsets to help increase service and improve regional connectivity, while at the same time reducing regional pollution and noise.” The train set will be on display at the LaSalle Street Station in Chicago today and tomorrow.

excerpt:
American Electric Power has agreed to buy up to 1.6 GW of Mainspring Energy’s linear generators over the next eight years, with an initial 190-MW delivery set for next year, the Menlo Park, California-based company said Tuesday. Under the agreement, which could be worth up to $4 billion, AEP will be able to buy about 200 MW a year, with the linear generating units expected to be online within 12 months, Tom Linebarger, Mainspring chairman and CEO, said Tuesday in an interview with Bloomberg Tech.
